method: Read of src/agents/tool.py, src/agents/run_state.py, src/agents/_tool_invocation.py, src/agents/memory/sqlite_session.py and src/agents/memory/openai_responses_compaction_session.py at 89c02c8, cloned from the public repository. Line numbers are that commit's.
notes: This is the first system assessed here that gates actions, so it is the first with anything to say at TR-3, and the shape of the answer is consistent: the SDK knows a great deal about WHAT was proposed and almost nothing about WHO allowed it. Tools carry needs_approval set in developer code, a run keeps a canonical ledger of tool invocations recording whether each executed, and a rejection can carry a reason. But approve() takes no approver, and the only thing called an identity in the approval path identifies the tool call rather than a person. The other half of the picture is the session layer, where the default store is append-only but the optional compaction session clears the whole history and writes back a model-written summary in its place. Both observations describe an SDK doing its job: it is a framework for building agents, not a record of what they did, and it does not claim otherwise.

evidence.note: the messages table stores created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP alongside message_data, so the write time is held with the item
the default session only appends items, so there is no in-place change for a previous version to survive
the compaction session calls underlying_session.clear_session() and then add_items(output_items), so the turns that were summarised are no longer readable afterwards

R1.2.note: In the default session there is nothing to preserve, because nothing changes. Where a session does change, in compaction, the prior state is destroyed rather than superseded.

evidence.note: the ordinary write is an append; nothing is edited in place

R1.3.note: The default path appends and is clean. What makes this partial is that a supported and automatic path destroys: with the compaction session, reaching the item threshold clears the session and replaces it with a summary, so the conversation an auditor would want to read is gone by design rather than by accident.

R2.2.note: Model-written content in the history is labelled as model-written. That is the whole of what this requirement asks, and the SDK does it.

evidence.note: the single match is an unrelated code comment at run_state.py:2514; there is no notion of a proposition, so there is nothing that could disagree
the session is an ordered list of conversation items; two statements that contradict each other are simply two items

R2.3.note: This is a consequence of the SDK storing conversation rather than belief. Both statements survive as text, but nothing in the system can tell that they are about the same thing, so nothing is retained as a disagreement.

evidence.note: no conflict type, record or query surface exists anywhere in the package
the default session never resolves anything: both statements stay in the log and neither is preferred, which is the conservative behaviour this requirement allows
compaction replaces a stretch of history with a model-written summary, which can silently reconcile or drop a disagreement, and records neither that it did so nor what it dropped

R2.5.note: Never resolving would be a pass. Compaction is the exception: it is the one place where an earlier statement can quietly stop being part of the record, decided by a model, with nothing written down about the decision.

evidence.note: a canonical per-run ledger records each call id with its type, approval scope, fingerprint, and whether it executed and completed. An attempted call that never ran is present in it
approvals and rejections serialise alongside, including rejection messages
no persistence layer writes the ledger anywhere; RunState serialises to JSON on request and it is the application's job to keep it

R3.1.note: The information exists and is well modelled, which is most of the work. What it is not is durable: the ledger lives in a run object, and whether it survives the process is a decision the SDK leaves to whoever embeds it.

evidence.note: needs_approval is declared on the tool, as a bool or a callable, and the docstring states the call must be approved via RunState.approve() or rejected via RunState.reject() before continuing
the function_tool decorator takes needs_approval and passes it into the constructed tool, so it is fixed in developer code at definition time

R3.2.note: This is a boolean gate rather than a graded risk class, but the substance the requirement asks for is met: whether an action needs approval is decided outside anything the model writes, and the model cannot clear its own gate.

evidence.note: the approvals record carries rejected alongside approved, per tool, with the same standing
the invocation ledger separates executed from completed, so a call stopped before execution is distinguishable from one that ran

R3.3.note: Refusals are modelled as faithfully as permissions, and the same caveat applies as at R3.1: this lives in the run state, not in a record that outlives it.
